topic: Gilbert & Ebert (2002) Harvard Photography Darkroom Choice Paradox: Why Keeping a 5-Day Swap Option Ruins Satisfaction with Your Own Pick

primary_case.title: Harvard Photography Darkroom Reversible vs Final Print Choice Experiment & Gourmet Jam Choice-Overload Field Study
primary_case.place: Department of Psychology, Harvard University (Cambridge, Massachusetts) & Upscale California Market
primary_case.summary: Gilbert & Ebert (2002) had Harvard photography students print two favorite black-and-white photos and pick one to take home either permanently or with a 5-day swap window. Although 66.3% of people asked beforehand preferred a reversible deal, students given 5 days to swap liked their print significantly less than students locked into a final pick, mirroring Iyengar & Lepper's (2000) 6-jar (30% buyers) vs 24-jar (3% buyers) choice trap.

core_facts.fact: In Gilbert & Ebert (2002 Journal of Personality and Social Psychology), Harvard University students enrolled in a hands-on photography darkroom course developed rolls of black-and-white film and printed two favorite portraits.

Harvard students had to choose one framed print to take home and give the second print away: one group made a permanent final choice on the spot, while the second group got 5 days to swap their print if they changed their mind.
When Gilbert & Ebert (2002) asked participants beforehand which rule they wanted, 66.3% (roughly 66 percent, two out of three students) chose the changeable swap deal over a final commitment.
Days later in Gilbert & Ebert (2002), students given the changeable swap option liked their chosen photo significantly less than students whose choice was final and unchangeable from minute one.

In Iyengar & Lepper's (2000 Journal of Personality and Social Psychology) gourmet market study, shoppers saw either 6 jars or 24 jars of jam: 30% of visitors at the 6-jar booth bought a jar, whereas only 3% at the 24-jar booth bought one.

Shenhav, Straccia, Cohen & Botvinick (2014 Nature Neuroscience) demonstrated with human fMRI that unresolved alternatives keep the anterior cingulate cortex firing to flag ongoing choice conflict and difficulty.

Voigt, Murawski, Speer & Bode (2019 Journal of Neuroscience; 2020 Human Brain Mapping) showed with human fMRI that committing to a final hard decision engages the prefrontal cortex alongside anterior cingulate networks to upgrade the value of the chosen option.

Chernev, Bockenholt & Goodman (2015 Journal of Consumer Psychology) confirmed across 99 choice-overload studies that unclosed trade-offs erode satisfaction unless a clear commitment closes comparison loops.

wow_facts.fact: 66.3% of Harvard participants asked for the reversible swap option beforehand, yet having 5 days to swap made students like their own chosen photo significantly less.
wow_facts.why_surprising: People crave an escape hatch for safety, unaware that the escape hatch blocks the brain's satisfaction builder.

wow_facts.fact: Displaying 24 gourmet jams instead of 6 slashed real store purchases tenfold from 30% down to 3%.
wow_facts.why_surprising: More options attract eyes but paralyze commitment.

wow_facts.fact: Human fMRI proves your prefrontal cortex upgrades how much you love a hard pick only after the decision locks for good.
wow_facts.why_surprising: Satisfaction is actively built after commitment, not passively discovered while shopping.

everyday_hooks: Keeping 30-day return receipts, free-cancellation buttons, and backup shopping tabs open — then nitpicking the very item you brought home.
Standing in front of 24 flavors or endless streaming thumbnails and walking away less satisfied than when you only had 6 solid picks.
